extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychology, psychoanalysis, literary theory, and humor studies
extracted.subtask_description: The page provides a psychoanalytic/theoretical account of what produces wit and the various forms of the comic, describing mechanisms (inhibition, expenditure, ideational mimicry), distinctions (wit vs. comic vs. naïve), and techniques for producing comic effect. It is aimed at analyzing and explaining humor rather than giving prescriptive jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit is essentially social and requires intelligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: “Wit ... is the most social of all those psychic functions whose aim is to gain pleasure. It often requires three persons ... It must therefore bind itself to the condition of intelligibleness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wit depends on at least one other person (often three roles: producer, second person, third person) and must be decipherable by that third person; unconscious mechanisms (condensation, displacement) can be used only to the extent that they remain intelligible to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: wit is made, the comic is found
rubrics_metrics.description: “Wit is made, while the comical is found; it is found first of all in persons, and only later by transference may be seen also in objects, situations, and the like.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wit is an intentional production employing techniques to obtain pleasure; the comic often arises unintentionally from perceived features of people or situations. This distinction guides whether to aim to construct a witty remark or to exploit found comic material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit's affective basis: removal of inhibition and word/nonsense pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit’s pleasure has a kernel of word-pleasure and nonsense-pleasure, and a shell of removal- and release-pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful wit combines intrinsic verbal play (sound, meaning mistakes) with a secondary pleasure from suspending or bypassing the censor/inhibition; producers and recipients must have comparable inhibitions for the affective effect to arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naïve as a form of the comic depending on perceived lack of inhibition
rubrics_metrics.description: The naïve “must result without our intervention ... The naïve originates when one puts himself completely outside of inhibition ... What conditions the function of the naïve is the fact that we are aware that the person does not possess this inhibition.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naïveté produces laughter when the audience perceives the speaker’s genuine lack of censor/inhibition (e.g., children’s remarks). The pleasure arises from economized inhibition expenditure in the hearer and from imaginatively placing oneself in the producer’s psychic state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naïve vs. wit: role of producer’s intent and audience’s assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Difference hinges on whether we assume the speaker intended a witticism or believed his statement in good faith; only the latter is naïveté.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar techniques/wording can read as either wit or naïveté depending on whether the audience attributes deliberate intent; to produce naïveté you must signal innocence/ignorance rather than clever intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques to make a person comical (production methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The means which serve to make a person comical are transference into comic situations, imitations, disguise, unmasking, caricature, parody, travesty, and the like.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These methods can be employed intentionally to create comic effect, but they may also serve hostile or aggressive aims (to render someone contemptible or deprive them of dignity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic originates as unintentional discovery in social relations
rubrics_metrics.description: “The comical appears primarily as an unintentional discovery in the social relations of human beings. It is found in persons, that is, in their movements, shapes, actions, and characteristic traits.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comical material is commonly discovered in observed human behavior and can be analyzed or deliberately staged once the conditions producing the comic are understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of motion: immoderate or inappropriate movements produce laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: “We laugh ... because we compare the motions observed in others with those which we ourselves should produce ... they appear to us immoderate and inappropriate; that is, we really laugh over the excessive expenditure of energy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perceivers simulate or ‘feel into’ observed motion (ideational mimicry) and detect surplus innervation/expenditure; exaggerated gestures, purposeless motions, or imitative over-effort (e.g., clowning, exaggerated grimaces) trigger comic response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideational mimicry: idea-conception accompanied by innervation
rubrics_metrics.description: “Even while an idea is in the process of conception innervations proceed to the muscles ... this expenditure of innervation ... represents the quantitative factor of the idea.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People naturally express magnitude and intensity in imagined content via bodily gestures, voice, or facial expression; vivid externalization of ideational content amplifies comic perception because observers compare those internal innervational cues with their own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure arises from comparison of two expenditures (identification vs. ego)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic pleasure results from comparing the other’s identification-expenditure with one’s own normal expenditure; when a surplus becomes inapplicable it is discharged as laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy can be analyzed as an economizing/discharge of psychic energy: if an observed action mobilizes more (or less) expenditure than expected, the difference can become available for pleasurable discharge (laughter) if conditions allow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of psychic attributes: foolish economizing of mental effort
rubrics_metrics.description: “In the case of the comic found in the mental and psychic attributes of another person ... it is comical if the other person economizes in expenditure, which I consider indispensable; for nonsense and foolishness are nothing but inferior activities.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whereas motion-based comic stems from excessive expenditure, psychic/foolishness-based comic stems from perceived under-expenditure of mental effort; the resulting pleasure often includes a felt superiority by the observer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of situation: identification with a changed energy-distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: “We laugh when we admit to ourselves that had we been placed in the same situation we should have done the same thing ... we draw the comic from the relation of the individual to the often all-too-powerful outer world.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situational comedy depends on recognizing a change in the subject’s mobilization of psychic energy (e.g., sudden pain, interruption) and being able to identify with that change at a distance (we do not feel the painful embarrassment ourselves).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of expectation: surplus from disappointed anticipatory mobilization
rubrics_metrics.description: “A quantitatively determined expenditure underlies our every idea of expectation ... If the ball turns out to be light ... I allowed myself to be misled by the expectation to exert an immoderate expenditure of motion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipatory motor preparations (tension, pre-mobilization) create measurable expenditure; when expectation is frustrated, the unspent or misapplied expenditure shows itself as comical—useful as a device in staged humor (e.g., pratfalls, false heaviness/hollowness).

rubrics_metrics.name: The role of comparison and identification in comic pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: “A comparison is indispensable ... this comparison between two energy expenditures which rapidly follow each other and refer to the same function ... is produced either in ourselves by way of identification with the other, or we find it ... in our own psychic processes.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether the comic is produced by identifying with another or by contrasting successive states within ourselves, the key mechanism is comparing two expenditures; design of comic material should create a clear, quickly apprehended comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic can be aggressive: making someone comical to demean them
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is quite evident that these techniques may enter into the service of hostile or aggressive tendencies. A person may be made comical in order to render him contemptible ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers of comic effect should be aware that techniques (caricature, unmasking, parody) can serve to humiliate; ethical/contextual considerations matter when deploying such methods.
